Want
wŏnt
n. and v. (deficiency, lack; to be destitute of; rendering Hebrew chaser, machsor)
From Old Norse vant, lacking. The Authorized Version uses want in its older and stronger sense — not desire, but deficiency — and the difference governs the most quoted verse in the Psalter.

Biblical Definition

Want in the Authorized Version means lack, not wish, and Psalm 23:1 turns on it: “The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want” — not I shall get whatever I desire, but I shall lack nothing the Shepherd judges necessary. Read as modern English it becomes a promise of indulgence; read as the translators meant it, it is a promise of sufficiency, which is far better and far harder. Psalm 34:10 supplies the same doctrine with a memorable contrast: “The young lions do lack, and suffer hunger: but they that seek the LORD shall not want any good thing” — the strongest hunters go short while the seekers are supplied, and the qualifier any good thing is God's definition of good, not ours. The word also carries covenant curse: Deuteronomy threatens service to enemies “in want of all things” (Deu 28:48). And Job, at his most desolate, names the want of a shelter (Job 24:8).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines want first as deficiency — the absence of that which is necessary or useful — and only afterward as desire or wish, marking the older sense as primary.

expand to see more

WANT, n. Deficiency; defect; the absence of that which is necessary or useful.

2. Need; necessity; the effect of deficiency.

3. Poverty; penury; indigence.

4. The state of not having. 5. That which is not possessed, but is desired or necessary.

Key Scripture

Psa 23:1 — "A Psalm of David. The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want."

Psa 34:10 — "The young lions do lack, and suffer hunger: but they that seek the LORD shall not want any good thing."

Deu 28:48 — "Therefore shalt thou serve thine enemies which the LORD shall send against thee, in hunger, and in thirst, and in nakedness, and in want of all things: and he shall put a yoke of iron upon thy neck, until he have destroyed thee."

Job 24:8 — "They are wet with the showers of the mountains, and embrace the rock for want of a shelter."

Modern Corruption

The semantic drift of one English word turning Psalm 23 into a promise of appetite satisfied — the exegetical root of the prosperity gospel, read straight out of a mistranslation the reader makes for himself.

expand to see more

This is a rare case where a corruption enters not by bad theology but by ordinary language change. In 1611 want meant lack; in modern English it means desire. A reader who supplies today's sense to Psalm 23:1 hears a guarantee that he will never be denied what he wants, and from there the prosperity gospel is only a short step — a divine Shepherd contracted to supply appetites. The Hebrew forecloses it: lo echsar, I shall not lack. Sufficiency, not indulgence.

The corrected reading is far more comforting, because it holds in a hospital and a famine. The sheep does not lack anything the Shepherd knows it needs, which is compatible with lying down in a valley of the shadow of death, and Psalm 34:10 attaches the same qualifier — any good thing, as God reckons good. Deuteronomy 28:48 shows the true opposite of the promise: not unfulfilled desire, but a people serving their enemies in want of all things.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew chaser (H2637), to lack, be without — the verb of Psa 23:1; machsor (H4270), need, poverty; Greek hustereo (G5302), to come short.

expand to see more

Hebrew chaser (H2637) — to lack, decrease, be without; lo echsar, I shall not lack (Psa 23:1), the same verb as the manna that left no lack (Exo 16:18).

Hebrew machsor (H4270) — need, want, poverty; what Proverbs promises the slack hand and the hasty man alike.

Greek hustereo (G5302) — to fall short, be destitute; Paul's I have learned… both to abound and to suffer need (Php 4:12).

Usage

"“The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want” — I shall not lack; the promise is sufficiency."

"“The young lions do lack… but they that seek the LORD shall not want any good thing” — and He defines good."

"“In hunger, and in thirst… and in want of all things” — the covenant curse."
